title: TypeScript SDK: dual-queue handshake for AsyncIterator <-> Web Streams interop
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Problem statement:
Teams building on the TypeScript SDK are repeatedly hitting ergonomics and correctness issues when bridging between AsyncIterator-style consumers (for await) and browser/node Web Streams (ReadableStream) producers. Common failures include dropped cancellation signals, lost backpressure semantics (leading to unbounded buffering), and brittle resume behavior after transient network errors.

Proposal summary:
Implement a small, well-documented runtime primitive (dual-queue handshake) that provides a deterministic mapping between AsyncIterator and ReadableStream semantics. The primitive is: a lightweight adapter that maintains two linked queues (pull queue and push queue) and a handshake token exchanged on each item to coordinate backpressure and cancellation.

Goals / acceptance criteria:
- Correctly propagate cancellation from either side (AsyncIterable consumer or ReadableStream reader) to the other side within one tick.
- Preserve backpressure: if the consumer is slow, the adapter should signal the upstream to pause producing (or buffer only up to a bounded limit) and expose an ergonomic API for configuring buffer limits and timeouts.
- Allow seamless conversion helpers: fromReadableStream(), toReadableStream(), fromAsyncIterable(), toAsyncIterable(). Helpers must be zero-copy where possible and document when buffering/serialization occurs.
- Provide clear retry/cancellation patterns for resumable streaming RPCs (examples for Redwood runtime RPCs).
- Unit and integration tests cover cancellation, error propagation, backpressure under load, swap (hot-swap) adapters, and restart after transient network disconnects.
- Performance regression target: adapter overhead <2ms per operation in microbenchmarks and <5% p99 increase in real workload traces.

Design details (high-level):
1) Dual queues:
   - pushQueue: holds items produced by upstream (ReadableStream or async producer) waiting for the consumer.
   - pullQueue: holds pending pull requests from a slow producer and fast consumer; each pull request includes a promise resolver.
   - handshake token per item: a tiny object containing { seq: number, cancel: () => void } used only for coordination and diagnostics.

2) Flow rules:
   - On produce(item): if pullQueue has waiters, resolve one waiter with item+handshake; otherwise push into pushQueue until buffer limit.
   - On consume(): if pushQueue has items, deliver next item and send immediate ack via handshake; otherwise push a waiter into pullQueue that will be resolved by next produce.
   - Cancellation: cancel() invoked from either side drains related queue entries, rejects outstanding promises with a dedicated error type (SDKStreamCancelledError), and notifies the other side through handshake.cancel().

3) Backpressure config:
   - constructor accepts options: { maxBufferItems: number, maxBufferBytes?: number, idleTimeoutMs?: number }
   - When maxBufferItems is reached, produce() will optionally await until space is available or throw if non-blocking mode configured. This lets consumers control memory/latency trade-offs.

4) Retry ergonomics:
   - Expose a small helper that composes the adapter with a retry policy for transient network errors: retrying will re-establish the producer stream and replay non-committal checkpoints (prefix caching, not item-level). The helper should clearly document when items are idempotent and when duplicates may occur.

API sketch (TypeScript):

interface Handshake<T> { seq: number; cancel: () => void; item: T }

class DualQueueAdapter<T> {
  constructor(options?: { maxBufferItems?: number; idleTimeoutMs?: number });
  push(item: T): Promise<void>; // called by producer
  pull(): Promise<Handshake<T>>; // called by consumer
  cancel(reason?: string): void; // immediate cancellation from either side
  toReadableStream(): ReadableStream<T>;
  toAsyncIterable(): AsyncIterable<T>;
  static fromReadableStream(s: ReadableStream<T>, options?): DualQueueAdapter<T>;
  static fromAsyncIterable(it: AsyncIterable<T>, options?): DualQueueAdapter<T>;
}

Examples (usage patterns):
- Server RPC -> Web Stream (browser): runtime exposes ReadableStream; browser wants async for-await usage. Use DualQueueAdapter.fromReadableStream(rts).toAsyncIterable().
- Client: for await consumer with backpressure-sensitive upstream: create adapter and give adapter.toReadableStream() to runtime; consumer uses for await on adapter.toAsyncIterable().

Edge cases and trade-offs:
- We intentionally avoid providing perfect at-most-once semantics for arbitrary user-provided iterables. If users need stronger guarantees they must couple with idempotency tokens at the application layer or use the Redwood prefix cache features.
- Buffer limits trade throughput for memory safety; defaults should be conservative (e.g., maxBufferItems=32).
- In environments without native ReadableStream (older Node versions), fall back to a tiny polyfill that wraps the adapter APIs. Include a migration note.

Testing plan:
- Unit: adapter state transitions (empty->buffered->full->cancelled), handshake seq monotonicity, cancellation propagation and message content.
- Integration: local loopback test connecting a Node runtime mock to browser-style reader and verifying timing/backpressure.
- Load: synthetic producers pushing at 10k items/s with consumer consuming at variable rates to ensure adapter enforces buffer limits and does not OOM.
- Fuzz: randomized cancellation during active handshake to catch race conditions.

Documentation and examples:
- Add a new docs page in the SDK site: "TypeScript streaming: AsyncIterator vs Web Streams" with migration steps and annotated examples.
- Provide a sample repo under /examples/ts/streaming-dual-queue showing runtime->browser, browser->runtime, and retry helper usage.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default buffer sizing strategy: fixed items vs adaptive bytes-based. Proposal: start with fixed items, add bytes later if customers request.
- Should produce() block by default when buffer is full, or throw? Proposal: block by default but allow non-blocking option for advanced users.

Acceptance checklist (developer-facing):
- [ ] Prototype implemented in SDK playground (branch: feat/stream-dual-queue)
- [ ] Unit/integration/load tests added
- [ ] API review with SDK maintainers and infra (doc + typings)
- [ ] Migration doc and example repository added
- [ ] Performance microbenchmarks committed and CI threshold defined
